title: catalogue randomness
content_html:
Catalogue Randomness

The Catalogue page provides an option [[icon:dices]] to shuffle the list of works displayed. This allows you to explore the catalogue in a random way. Whilst simple browser based seeded random number generation would produce the desired effect, here we have chosen to use a method of generating random numbers closer to the spirit of work .

From quantum measurements to files

A quantum random bit generator (QRBG) converts measurements of a quantum process into a stream of random bits. The LfD laboratory exposes the output of its ID Quantique Quantis PCIe hardware through an API that takes a length in bytes. Each byte contains eight bits. With format=HEX, the API returns a JSON response whose qrn field represents each byte as two hexadecimal digits. For example, 46 represents the byte 01000110. (see LfD QRNG API)

On 2026-11-12, we fetched 2,097,152 bytes (2 MiB) in one request. We decoded the hex and split the resulting stream in order into 64 consecutive files of 32,768 bytes (32 KiB) each. The files run from 01.bin through 64.bin. Each file starts directly with the random bytes. The file size and the grouping of bytes into numbers are choices made by Catalogue. Another consumer could read the same bytes in groups of a different size.

From bytes to shuffle draws

Clicking the dice uses JavaScript's Math.random() to choose one of the 64 files. The browser fetches that file from the site's own origin and reads it four bytes at a time, most significant byte first. Each group gives one unsigned 32-bit integer in the range 0 to 4,294,967,295, so each file supplies 8,192 candidate draws. The first four bytes of the original 01.bin are 46 98 58 70. Together they make the integer 0x46985870, or 1,184,389,232 in decimal.

Fisher–Yates starts at the last slot and works backward through the list. At each step, it selects one of the remaining Works, including the Work already in that slot, and swaps the selected Work into place. A shuffle of n Works needs n − 1 accepted draws because the final Work is already in place.

The range of a 32-bit integer does not always divide evenly by the number of remaining Works. With ten Works left, for example, 2³² leaves a remainder of six when divided by ten. Catalogue skips the six highest values and takes the remainder modulo ten for each accepted value. Each slot then has the same number of input values that select it. A draw of 1,184,389,232 would pick index 2, the third remaining slot.

The first row of 01.bin

The first row of the 64 × 64 bit grid shows the first eight bytes of 01.bin, 46 98 58 70 94 d4 93 cd. Those 64 bits give two draws. Using the repository's public Catalogue snapshot of 5,196 Works in its default order, both draws were accepted and fixed the last two slots. Slot numbers below start at 1.

Draw Remaining Works Slot picked Work Final slot
1,184,389,232 5,196 2,601 04169 · form 61 5,196
2,496,959,437 5,195 3,468 00393 · model 500 5,195

Each draw selects a slot, and the entry at that slot supplies the Work ID. The first swap moved 04435 to slot 2,601 and the second moved 04433 to slot 3,468. Later draws could still move those two Works.

Capacity and repeatability

The error The shuffle batch ran out of draws for this Catalogue means the browser reached the end of the file while it still needed another accepted draw. At 5,196 Works, a shuffle needs 5,195 accepted draws and can spare up to 2,997 rejections. At 8,193 Works, every draw has to be accepted. At 8,194 Works or more, the file is always too small. This is something I will address should I ever get to that point...

The same file and starting Work order reproduce the same shuffle. For a fixed starting order and stock, the 64 files can produce up to 64 distinct permutations. Catalogue saves the selected file number and page for the tab session, so a refresh or a return through the collection icon can recreate the order. A change to the file or the starting Work order can produce a different result. The browser uses ordinary HTTP caching when it reads the file again.
